about: A 15-credit Term 2 module for first-year BSc Politics and International Relations students on how modern states make and deliver public policy. The 2026/27 catalogue describes it as covering theories of decision making and the roles of the actors who try to steer policy: public opinion, politicians, lobbyists and bureaucrats. Assessment is listed as 90% viva or oral presentation and 10% in-class activity. This pack adds a topic on the policy process (stages, multiple streams, punctuated equilibrium) and on implementation, because these are standard parts of how decision-making theories and bureaucratic roles are taught; check your reading list for the emphasis your seminars take.

notes.h: Theories of decision making: rationality, bounded rationality, incrementalism and nudges
notes.body:
Policy making is a series of decisions: whether to act, what to do and how. Theories of decision making offer rival pictures of how those choices are, or should be, made.

The rational comprehensive model
The classic ideal has the decision-maker define the problem, clarify goals and rank them, list all alternatives, predict the consequences of each, and select the option that best achieves the goals. Cost-benefit analysis is its practical form. In the UK, HM Treasury's Green Book sets out how to appraise policies by comparing costs and benefits over time. Future values are discounted, because benefits that arrive later are worth less to us now. For example, at a 3% discount rate £100 of benefit arriving in ten years is worth £100/1.03¹⁰ ≈ £74.41 today. At the time of writing (November 2026), the Green Book's standard rate (the social time preference rate) is 3% in real terms for the first 30 years: the Treasury cut it from 3.5% (at which the same £100 would be worth about £70.89) in October 2026, after an independent review published in June 2026 recommended 3%. Check current Treasury guidance for the latest rate.

Bounded rationality and satisficing
Simon (Administrative Behavior, 1947; 'A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice', 1955) argued that people have limited information, time and cognitive capacity, so they are boundedly rational. Rather than maximising, they satisfice: they search until they find an option that meets an acceptable threshold and then stop. Organisations simplify with routines and rules of thumb.

Incrementalism
Lindblom ('The Science of "Muddling Through"', Public Administration Review, 1959) contrasted the rational comprehensive 'root' method with the 'branch' method of successive limited comparisons. Policy makers, he argued, usually make small adjustments to existing policy, compare only a few alternatives that differ marginally from the status quo, and fix mistakes as they go. Goals and means are chosen together, and agreement among political actors on a policy matters more than agreement on abstract goals. Strengths: realistic, lowers risk and fits pluralist bargaining. Criticisms: it favours the status quo, struggles with large problems that need a step change, and may neglect those without a voice. Etzioni (1967) proposed mixed scanning, using a broad view for fundamental decisions and an incremental one for details.

The garbage can model
Cohen, March and Olsen (1972) described 'organised anarchies' with unclear goals, uncertain methods and fluid participation. In their model, problems, solutions, participants and choice opportunities flow independently, and decisions occur when they happen to meet. Solutions can look for problems rather than the reverse. This idea was developed in Kingdon's multiple streams framework.

Allison's three models
Allison (Essence of Decision, 1971), studying the Cuban missile crisis, compared the rational actor model, the organisational process model (outcomes follow standard operating procedures) and the governmental politics model (outcomes result from bargaining among officials with different positions). The lesson is that the same event is explained differently depending on the lens.

Public choice
Public choice applies economic assumptions to politics. Downs (An Economic Theory of Democracy, 1957) argued that parties seek votes and that voters can be rationally ignorant because the cost of information outweighs the tiny chance their vote matters. Niskanen (1971) modelled bureaucrats as budget-maximisers; critics such as Dunleavy (1991) argued that officials prefer to shape their roles into more attractive tasks.

Behavioural approaches and nudges
Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) showed that people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point and weigh losses more heavily than equal gains. People rely on heuristics and are affected by framing and defaults. Thaler and Sunstein (Nudge, 2008) argued that policy makers can use choice architecture, the way options are presented, to steer decisions in predictable ways without forbidding options or significantly changing financial incentives. Their approach is 'libertarian paternalism'. Automatic enrolment in workplace pensions with the right to opt out is a standard example of a default; the UK Behavioural Insights Team was set up in the Cabinet Office in 2010 to apply such ideas. Critics argue that nudges can be manipulative, may not change behaviour much for large problems, and can distract from structural measures.

Exam tips: present each theory with its author, date and main claim; contrast what is descriptive (how decisions are made) and normative (how they should be); apply at least one theory to a policy example.

notes.h: The policy process: stages, streams and punctuated equilibrium
notes.body:
Theories of the policy process try to explain why some issues reach the agenda, how policy changes and why change is sometimes sudden. They sit within the broad topic of theories of decision making.

The stages (policy cycle) model
Lasswell (The Decision Process, 1956) divided the policy process into functional stages. Simplified versions have agenda setting, formulation, decision (adoption), implementation and evaluation, with feedback to the start. In the UK Treasury's Green Book the appraisal cycle is summarised as ROAMEF: rationale, objectives, appraisal, monitoring, evaluation and feedback. The stages model is a useful way to organise analysis, but it is a heuristic. Critics such as Sabatier (1999) argued that real policy making is not a neat sequence: stages overlap, implementation can reshape the policy, and the model offers no causal theory about why things happen.

Agenda setting and non-decisions
Not all problems get attention. Bachrach and Baratz (1962) argued that power has a second face: controlling the agenda so that some issues are never considered. In a follow-up article (1963) they called this non-decision making. Cobb and Elder (1972) studied how issues move from the public agenda to the formal agenda.

Kingdon's multiple streams
Kingdon (Agendas, Alternatives, and Public Policies, 1984) built on the garbage can model. He identified three largely independent streams:
- The problem stream: conditions that people define as problems, brought to attention by indicators, focusing events (crises, disasters) and feedback.
- The policy stream: the ideas and proposals circulating among specialists, which are developed and refined in a 'policy primeval soup'.
- The politics stream: the national mood, organised interests and changes of government or legislature.
A policy window opens briefly when a problem becomes pressing or a political change occurs. Policy entrepreneurs, who invest time and resources, then couple the streams by attaching a solution to a problem and finding political support. Without coupling, ideas wait. The framework explains why timing and chance matter, but it is hard to test and is sometimes seen as vague about when windows open.

Punctuated equilibrium
Baumgartner and Jones (Agendas and Instability in American Politics, 1993) argued that policy is marked by long periods of stability and incremental change, punctuated by short bursts of large change. Stability is held in place by policy monopolies, in which a dominant group controls the policy image (how the issue is understood) and the institutional venue (where it is decided) and negative feedback keeps things stable. Because attention is scarce, issues can suddenly attract attention; changes in the policy image or a move to a new venue can trigger positive feedback and rapid change. This explains both incrementalism (most of the time) and big shifts (occasionally). The pattern of policy changes is typically not normally distributed: many small changes and a few large ones.

Advocacy coalition framework
Sabatier and Jenkins-Smith (1993) proposed that policy within a subsystem is shaped by competing advocacy coalitions bound by shared beliefs. Beliefs are layered into deep core, policy core and secondary aspects. Policy-oriented learning typically changes secondary beliefs, while major change usually needs external shocks or long-term shifts.

Path dependence and policy feedback
Pierson (2000) argued that early decisions can set a path that becomes costly to reverse, because of increasing returns, such as sunk costs, expectations and organisations that grow up around a policy. Policies also change politics by creating beneficiaries who defend them.

Policy diffusion and transfer
Policies spread through learning, competition, emulation and coercion. Dolowitz and Marsh (2000) analysed policy transfer. A UK example is the spread of smoke-free enclosed public places: Scotland acted in 2006 and England followed in 2007.

Choosing between theories
They explain different things. Lindblom explains routine change, Baumgartner and Jones both stability and sudden change, Kingdon the timing of agenda access, and the advocacy coalition framework long-term change within subsystems.

Exam tips: identify the unit of explanation (individual, coalition, system); give the author, date and key concepts of each theory; use an example and note limitations of each.

In a democracy, policy is supposed to reflect the preferences of citizens. Studying public opinion asks how much citizens know, how their opinions form, how they are measured, and how far policy follows them.

What does the public know?
Early survey research was pessimistic. Converse (1964) argued that most citizens lack a stable, ideologically organised belief system: many give inconsistent answers over time, which he later (1970) described as 'non-attitudes'. Downs (1957) gave a rational-choice explanation: because one vote has a tiny chance of deciding an election, citizens have little incentive to learn about policy, so they are rationally ignorant. Later work argues that citizens use cues and heuristics, such as party labels or trusted endorsers, to form reasonable choices (Lupia, 1994), and that aggregated opinion can be more stable and sensible than individual opinion (Page and Shapiro, 1992).

How opinions form
Zaller (The Nature and Origins of Mass Opinion, 1992) proposed that people receive political messages from elites, accept those consistent with their values, and answer survey questions using whichever considerations are at the top of their mind when asked. This explains why question wording and framing matter. Framing effects occur when different descriptions of the same issue change opinions, as in 'tax relief' compared with 'tax cuts for the rich'.

Measuring opinion
Opinion polls estimate views from a sample, and are affected by sampling error (poll margin of about ±3 points for a random sample of 1,000), non-response, question wording and social desirability. Salience matters: someone may favour a policy mildly but not vote on it. Referendums give a direct measure but only on questions put by governments, and results depend on framing and turnout. In the 2016 EU referendum Leave won 51.9% to 48.1% on a turnout of 72.2%. Deliberative methods such as citizens' assemblies seek considered opinion.

Does opinion influence policy?
- Page and Shapiro (1983) found that US policy changes were more often congruent with earlier changes in public opinion than not, especially for large and stable shifts.
- Wlezien (1995) proposed a thermostatic model: the public acts like a thermostat, wanting more spending when policy falls below its preferred level and less when it is above, so policy changes feed back into opinion.
- Stimson, MacKuen and Erikson (1995) described 'dynamic representation' in which policy moves in line with shifts in the public's overall liberal-conservative mood.
- Gilens and Page (2014) examined a large set of US policy issues and concluded that economic elites and organised business groups had substantial independent influence on policy, while the preferences of average citizens had little independent effect once those groups were controlled for. Their findings are contested by later critics who argue that preferences of different income groups often coincide and that measurement choices matter.
Congruence between opinion and policy does not prove causation. Policy may follow opinion, but opinion can also follow elite leadership or reflect past policy.

Elites leading opinion
Opinion does not always dictate policy. The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 suspended the death penalty for murder in Great Britain for five years, and abolition was made permanent in 1969, at a time when opinion polls generally showed public support for capital punishment, showing that parliamentary and elite leadership can move ahead of public opinion.

Why policy may diverge from opinion
Issue salience is low for most voters; institutional veto points and party competition shape outcomes; organised interests are more active than the diffuse public; and governments may have information or values that differ from the public's.

Exam tips: distinguish what the public wants, what it knows, and what it can influence; cite more than one study when assessing whether policy follows opinion; note that correlation between opinion and policy is not proof that opinion caused policy.

Politicians are the actors with formal authority to make policy. Understanding what they want, and what constrains them, helps explain which policies are chosen.

What do politicians want?
- Re-election: Mayhew (The Electoral Connection, 1974) assumed that US legislators are single-minded seekers of re-election, and showed how advertising, credit claiming and position taking serve that goal.
- Strøm (1990) distinguished parties that seek votes, office or policy, and argued that they trade these goals off.
- Downs (1957) modelled parties as vote-maximisers who converge on the median voter in a two-party competition on one dimension; real politics is multidimensional and parties also have principled and activist constraints.
- Politicians also pursue reputation, ideology and legacy, and need to avoid blame. Weaver (1986) argued that officeholders are often motivated more by avoiding blame than claiming credit, so they use strategies such as delegating or agenda limiting.

Mandates and representation
- Mandate theory: a winning party has authority to carry out its manifesto commitments. Critics note that election results do not show support for individual policies and that voters choose bundles.
- Delegate versus trustee: Burke's speech to the electors of Bristol (1774) argued that a representative owes constituents judgement, not blind obedience to their instructions. A delegate follows instructions; a trustee uses his or her own judgement.
- Pitkin (The Concept of Representation, 1967) distinguished formal, descriptive, symbolic and substantive representation. Mansbridge (2003) described promissory, anticipatory, gyroscopic and surrogate forms.
- In the UK, the voting system affects mandate claims. At the 2024 general election Labour won about 411 of 650 seats, around 63%, on 33.7% of the votes cast, an illustration of how a plurality system can turn a minority of votes into a majority of seats.

Institutions that constrain politicians
- Parliamentary systems such as the UK: the executive is drawn from the legislature, party discipline is strong, the Cabinet operates under collective responsibility and ministers are individually responsible to Parliament. The government normally controls much of the legislative agenda.
- Veto players: Tsebelis (Veto Players, 2002) defined a veto player as an actor whose agreement is needed to change the status quo. Policy stability increases with the number of veto players, the ideological distance between them and their internal cohesion. Coalition governments, bicameral systems and independent courts add veto players.
- Coalition government: partners must bargain; coalition agreements set policy compromises and portfolios.
- Courts, devolved governments, the Bank of England and international commitments limit or share decisions.

Electoral incentives and time
Short electoral horizons encourage policies that bring quick benefits and delay costs. Nordhaus (1975) modelled a political business cycle in which governments expand the economy before elections; evidence for it is mixed. In the UK the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 was repealed by the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022, restoring the power of the Prime Minister to ask for an early dissolution.

Policy leadership
Ministers set direction, but depend on civil servants for information and implementation. Special advisers, party research units and think tanks supply ideas. Policy entrepreneurs within politics can use windows of opportunity.

Blame and credit
Because losses loom larger than gains for voters (see behavioural theory), politicians may avoid visible costs, even for long-term benefits. Strategies include blaming other levels of government, delegating to independent agencies, or presenting cuts as technical.

Exam tips: link motives (re-election, office, policy) to concrete policy behaviour; use veto player logic to explain stability or change; avoid vague claims about 'politicians' without specifying institutions.

Lobbying means attempts by organised interests to influence policy decisions. It includes trade associations, businesses, unions, professional bodies, charities, campaign groups and the consultancies that represent them. Its role in democracy is contested: it may supply information and represent interests, but it can also give unequal influence to those with resources.

Types of groups
- Sectional (interest) groups defend the interests of members, such as a trade union or business association. Cause (promotional) groups promote a cause, such as an environmental campaign.
- Insider groups are consulted regularly by government and have routine access, often accepting constraints in exchange. Outsider groups lack such access and rely more on public campaigns and media pressure (the insider/outsider distinction developed by Wyn Grant from the late 1970s and set out in his Pressure Groups, Politics and Democracy in Britain, 1989). Some groups choose an outsider strategy deliberately.

Theories of group influence
- Pluralism (Dahl, Who Governs?, 1961): power is dispersed among many groups, no single group dominates, and government responds to competing pressures.
- Neo-pluralism: business has a privileged position because governments depend on investment and employment (Lindblom, Politics and Markets, 1977).
- Corporatism (Schmitter, 1974): a few peak associations are given official status in policy making and in return help to implement agreements.
- Policy communities and issue networks (Rhodes and Marsh, 1992): policy is made in specialised subsystems; policy communities are close, stable and resource-sharing, issue networks more open and unstable.
- Public choice and capture: Stigler (1971) argued that regulated industries often 'capture' regulators, shaping regulation to benefit themselves.

Collective action
Olson (The Logic of Collective Action, 1965) argued that rational individuals will not contribute to the provision of a collective good if they can free-ride, so large groups with diffuse benefits tend to under-organise, while small, concentrated groups, or groups offering selective incentives such as services to members, organise more easily. This predicts a bias towards concentrated interests, such as producers, over diffuse ones, such as consumers or taxpayers.

How lobbying works
- Providing information and expertise: Hall and Deardorff (2006) described lobbying as a 'legislative subsidy', supplying allies with research and arguments that reduce their costs of acting.
- Access: meetings, consultations (written consultations on proposals, such as green and white papers, and responses by organisations), evidence to parliamentary committees, advisory bodies and secondments.
- Public campaigns, media pressure and mobilising members.
- Financial support: donations and events; in the UK, the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 regulates donations and requires reporting to the Electoral Commission.
- The 'revolving door': officials and politicians moving to private jobs. In the UK the Advisory Committee on Business Appointments advises on such moves.

How much influence do they have?
Influence is hard to measure, since access is not the same as influence, and the aim of a group may be to block change. Baumgartner and colleagues (Lobbying and Policy Change, 2009) examined 98 issues in the United States and found that the side with more resources was not clearly more likely to win; the status quo advantage was a stronger factor: groups defending the status quo usually did better than those seeking change. Dür (2008) argued that estimates of influence require careful comparison of preferences and outcomes. Influence can also operate through anticipated reactions and agenda control.

Regulation of lobbying in the UK
The Transparency of Lobbying, Non-Party Campaigning and Trade Union Administration Act 2014 created a Register of Consultant Lobbyists, but it covers only consultant lobbyists (those lobbying on behalf of third parties), not in-house lobbyists, which critics say leaves much lobbying undisclosed. The Ministerial Code and rules on meetings and gifts add further regulation.

Normative questions
Lobbying can enhance representation and information, but unequal access, secrecy and conflicts of interest threaten equality and trust. Remedies include transparency registers, cooling-off periods and limits on donations.

Exam tips: define insider versus outsider carefully; apply Olson's logic to a concrete case; discuss influence as hard to measure, and cite evidence on both sides.

Bureaucrats are the permanent officials who advise on, administer and deliver public policy. Their role raises two questions: do they control policy, and how is policy changed on the way from decision to delivery?

The classic model
Weber (Economy and Society, published 1922) described the ideal-type bureaucracy: hierarchy, fixed rules, specialised functions, impersonal procedures, written records and appointment and promotion on merit with a career structure. He viewed it as technically efficient but warned of the costs of rationalisation, an idea he captured in the image of an 'iron cage'. In Britain, the Northcote–Trevelyan Report (1854) argued for recruitment by open competition on merit, a permanent, politically neutral civil service. The Civil Service Code states the values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 gave the civil service a statutory basis.

Politicians and bureaucrats
Aberbach, Putnam and Rockman (Bureaucrats and Politicians in Western Democracies, 1981) described images of their relationship, from a strict separation (politicians decide, officials execute) to a 'pure hybrid' in which both engage in policy and politics. Officials advise ministers, shape options and control information. Ministers decide, but depend on officials' expertise. Wildavsky (Speaking Truth to Power, 1979) discussed the tension between analysis and politics. Principal–agent theory describes ministers as principals and officials as agents who have their own interests and an information advantage; the principal's tools include monitoring, incentives and appointments.

Public choice views
Niskanen (Bureaucracy and Representative Government, 1971) modelled bureaucrats as budget-maximisers who expand their agencies. Dunleavy (Democracy, Bureaucracy and Public Choice, 1991) argued that senior officials prefer to 'bureau-shape': restructuring so that they do more interesting, policy-focused work, delegating routine tasks to agencies, rather than maximising budgets. Wilson (Bureaucracy, 1989) emphasised that agencies' behaviour depends on their tasks and organisational culture.

Delegation and independent bodies
Governments delegate to arm's-length agencies and regulators to gain expertise and credibility. Kydland and Prescott (1977) showed why governments may want to tie their hands: promises about low inflation are not credible if politicians can later change their minds. The Bank of England was given operational independence in 1997 to set interest rates to meet the government's inflation target, an illustration of delegating to improve credible commitment. The Next Steps report (1988) led to executive agencies in the UK. New Public Management (Hood, 1991) promoted performance targets, markets and disaggregation.

Implementation
Policies can fail between decision and delivery.
- Top-down view: Pressman and Wildavsky (Implementation, 1973) studied a federal programme in Oakland and argued that a programme depending on many separate agreements or clearances (complexity of joint action) is likely to fail. Even if each step has a high chance of success, the chances multiply. For example, if a programme needed 70 independent clearances and each had a 99% chance of agreement, the probability that all succeed would be 0.99⁷⁰ ≈ 0.495, about 50%. Hogwood and Gunn (1984) listed conditions for 'perfect implementation' (clear objectives, adequate resources, minimal dependencies). Mazmanian and Sabatier (1983) emphasised clear legal objectives and committed implementers.
- Bottom-up view: Lipsky (Street-Level Bureaucracy, 1980) argued that frontline workers such as teachers, police, social workers and benefit officers have discretion and face high caseloads and limited resources. They develop routines, rationing and simplification to cope, so that the policy delivered is in effect shaped by their behaviour.
- Matland (1995) argued that the best approach depends on conflict and ambiguity: administrative implementation when both are low, political implementation when conflict is high, experimental when ambiguity is high, and symbolic when both are high.

Why it matters
Policy outcomes depend on delivery as well as design. Performance targets can lead to gaming (Goodhart's law). Outsourcing and networks raise accountability questions.

Exam tips: distinguish top-down from bottom-up; show the arithmetic in Pressman and Wildavsky-type questions; define discretion for Lipsky; use the principal–agent idea to discuss control of bureaucracy.

questions.q: What does Simon's idea of 'satisficing' say about decision makers?
options: They evaluate all possible alternatives and choose the one that maximises expected benefit
They choose the option that departs least from existing policy
They make decisions when problems, solutions and participants happen to meet in a choice opportunity
They search until they find an option that meets an acceptable threshold, because information and cognitive capacity are limited
questions.why: Satisficing means stopping the search at the first 'good enough' option, which follows from bounded rationality. Evaluating every alternative and maximising is the rational comprehensive model that Simon criticised. Choosing the smallest departure from the status quo describes Lindblom's incrementalism, a different theory. Decisions emerging when streams meet describes the garbage can model of Cohen, March and Olsen.

questions.q: What did Lindblom (1959) recommend, and describe, as the way policy is typically made?
options: Small changes from the status quo through successive limited comparisons, correcting mistakes as they appear
Comprehensive evaluation of all alternatives against agreed goals
Waiting for a policy window when the problem, policy and politics streams join
Using defaults and framing to steer individual choices
questions.why: The 'branch' method of successive limited comparisons is Lindblom's incrementalism. The comprehensive evaluation described in the distractor is the 'root' method, which he argued is not feasible in practice. The idea of streams joining at a policy window is Kingdon's multiple streams approach. Defaults and choice architecture belong to Thaler and Sunstein's nudge approach.

questions.q: Explain Lindblom's incrementalism and give two criticisms of it.
markScheme: Describes policy as small adjustments from status quo via successive limited comparisons (1959)
Contrasts with rational comprehensive 'root' method
Reasons: limited information, time, political agreement, ability to correct
Criticism: conservative, status quo bias; poor for major problems needing large change
Criticism: neglects those without a voice / may drift without direction
questions.modelAnswer: Lindblom (1959) argued that policy makers rarely follow the rational comprehensive method. Instead they use successive limited comparisons: they compare a few alternatives that differ only marginally from current policy, accept what political actors can agree on and revise as consequences emerge. This is realistic given limited information and time, and it makes reversing mistakes easier. One criticism is that it favours the status quo and is poorly suited to problems that require a step change, such as a rapid response to a new crisis. Another is that it tends to reflect the interests of those already represented in bargaining, so it may neglect groups without a voice, and a series of small steps can drift without any strategic direction.

questions.q: Which three streams does Kingdon (1984) identify in his multiple streams approach?
options: Inputs, outputs and feedback
Agenda setting, formulation and implementation
Problems, policies and politics
Ideas, interests and institutions
questions.why: Kingdon's streams are problems, policies and politics, which couple when a policy window opens. Inputs, outputs and feedback describe a systems model of politics, not Kingdon's framework. Agenda setting, formulation and implementation are stages of the policy cycle, a different way of organising the process. Ideas, interests and institutions are a common triad in institutional analysis but not Kingdon's three streams.

questions.q: What pattern of policy change does Baumgartner and Jones's punctuated equilibrium theory predict?
options: Gradual convergence on the best policy through learning
Steady incremental change at a constant pace
Long periods of stability and small changes, interrupted by occasional large shifts when attention and policy images change
A repeating fixed cycle through the same stages
questions.why: The theory expects mostly stability with occasional bursts of rapid change, giving a distribution with many small changes and a few large ones. Constant incremental change is what pure incrementalism would predict. A repeating cycle through stages is the policy cycle heuristic, which is not what punctuated equilibrium claims. Convergence on the best policy through learning is closer to rational or learning models and ignores the role of attention and venue.

questions.q: Using Kingdon's multiple streams framework, explain how a policy window might open and be used, with an example.
markScheme: Three streams: problem, policy, politics
Policy window opens through focusing event or political change
Role of policy entrepreneurs in coupling streams
Example applied sensibly
Limit: timing/chance; hard to test or predict windows
questions.modelAnswer: Kingdon describes three relatively independent streams: problems (conditions defined as needing action), policies (proposals developed by specialists) and politics (mood, interest groups, elections and changes of government). A policy window opens when a problem becomes pressing, for instance after a focusing event such as a disaster, or when the politics stream shifts, for instance after an election. Policy entrepreneurs, who have prepared solutions, take advantage by coupling a solution to the problem and gaining political support. For example, after a high-profile failure of a regulator, a prepared reform proposal may be attached to the demand for action. The approach explains the role of timing, but windows are brief and hard to predict, and the framework is difficult to test.

questions.q: What does Wlezien's thermostatic model (1995) say about public preferences for government spending?
options: They simply follow the position taken by the governing party
They keep rising in the direction of the most recent policy change
They adjust in response to policy: when spending rises above the preferred level, demand for more spending falls, and vice versa
They are fixed and unaffected by what the government actually does
questions.why: A thermostat registers the gap between actual and preferred levels, so opinion moves back as policy overshoots or undershoots. If preferences kept rising along with policy, there would be no feedback correction. Fixed preferences contradict the model, which is about opinion responding to policy. Simply following the governing party describes cue-taking, which is a different mechanism.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises Gilens and Page's (2014) main finding and its status?
options: Policy responds equally to the preferences of rich and poor citizens
Economic elites and organised business groups had substantial independent influence on US policy, while average citizens had little independent influence, a conclusion later contested
Average citizens' preferences determine US policy and elites have no independent influence
Interest groups have no independent effect once public opinion is controlled
questions.why: They reported that, controlling for each, elites and organised groups mattered while the average citizen's preferences had little independent effect. The reverse of this, with citizens determining policy, is the majoritarian picture that they argued is not supported. Interest groups mattering after controlling for opinion is also the opposite of their conclusion. Equal responsiveness to rich and poor is another prediction their analysis did not find.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim that policy makers follow public opinion. Refer to at least two studies or theories.
markScheme: Evidence of congruence (Page and Shapiro 1983; dynamic representation)
Thermostatic model: opinion responds to policy
Counter-evidence (Gilens and Page 2014, contested)
Causation unclear: elites shape opinion; low salience; death penalty example
Judgement
questions.modelAnswer: There is evidence that policy follows opinion: Page and Shapiro (1983) found US policy changes were more often congruent than not with earlier opinion shifts, and Stimson, MacKuen and Erikson (1995) described policy moving with the public mood. Wlezien's thermostatic model suggests an interaction, as opinion also responds to what policy does. Against this, Gilens and Page (2014) concluded that elites and organised groups had more independent influence than average citizens, although their finding has been disputed. Congruence may also reflect elite leadership of opinion rather than responsiveness, and opinion is often low in salience. The ending of the death penalty for murder in Great Britain (suspended in 1965, abolished permanently in 1969), despite public support for it, shows policy makers sometimes lead. Overall, opinion constrains policy in broad terms, especially on salient issues, but the link is partial.

questions.q: What did Burke argue in his speech to the electors of Bristol (1774)?
options: A representative must follow the instructions of constituents on every issue
A representative must always follow the party whip
A representative should maximise the chance of re-election above all
A representative should use independent judgement in the national interest, not simply obey constituents' instructions
questions.why: Burke's view is the trustee model: constituents are owed judgement, not obedience. Following instructions is the delegate model that he rejected. The party whip is a feature of party discipline, which Burke did not discuss in that way. Maximising re-election is closer to Mayhew's modern account of legislators' motives, and it is not what Burke recommended.

questions.q: According to Tsebelis's veto player theory, what happens to policy stability when there are more veto players whose preferences are far apart?
options: Policy stability increases, because it is harder to find a change that all veto players prefer to the status quo
Policy becomes more extreme, since each veto player pushes the outcome towards its own position
Policy change becomes easier because more actors can propose reforms
Stability depends only on the number of parties, not on how far apart their preferences are
questions.why: Each extra veto player, particularly one with distant preferences, shrinks the set of changes that everyone prefers to the status quo, so stability rises. Veto players block change; proposing reforms is a separate power, so more actors does not make change easier. Ideological distance and cohesion matter in the theory, not just the count of parties. The expected effect is gridlock around the status quo and not the extremes.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by a 'veto player' and illustrate how veto players affect policy change in the UK, with reference to one example of an additional veto player.
markScheme: Definition: actor whose agreement is needed to change the status quo
Stability increases with number, distance and cohesion
UK: single-party majority government has few veto players in the Commons
Examples: coalition partners, House of Lords (delaying), courts, devolved governments
Link to outcome: more veto players, more gridlock
questions.modelAnswer: A veto player (Tsebelis, 2002) is an actor whose agreement is required to change the status quo. Policy stability increases with the number of veto players, the ideological distance between them and their internal cohesion. In the UK a single-party majority government in the Commons has few veto players, so policy can change relatively easily. Additional veto players include a coalition partner, which must agree to legislation (as in 2010–15); backbench rebels when the majority is small; the House of Lords, which can delay and amend bills; and devolved governments on devolved matters. The more such actors with distinct preferences, the narrower the range of policies they can all prefer to the status quo.

questions.q: Why, according to Olson (1965), do small concentrated groups often organise more effectively than large diffuse ones?
options: Each member's share of the benefit is larger and free-riding is easier to detect, so collective action is easier to sustain
Free-riding is a problem only in small groups
Large groups never face collective action problems, because benefits are shared widely
Small groups always have more members and therefore more resources
questions.why: In a small group the per-member gain is large and non-contributors are visible, so organisation is easier. The claim that large groups never face collective action problems reverses Olson's argument, since the larger the group the stronger the free-rider problem. Small groups have fewer, not more, members. Free-riding is a bigger problem in large groups, because each person's contribution makes little difference and is hard to monitor.

questions.q: In Wyn Grant's insider/outsider typology, what is an 'insider' group?
options: A group whose members are government officials
A group that is consulted regularly by government and has routine access to policy makers
A group that relies mainly on protests and media campaigns because it lacks access
A sectional group representing business only
questions.why: Insider status is about relationship with government: regular consultation and access. Membership of government is not required, and officials do not form insider groups by definition. Relying on protest and media pressure is characteristic of outsider groups. The sectional–cause distinction is a separate classification, and insiders can be cause groups, such as charities consulted on policy.

questions.q: Outline three ways in which lobbyists seek to influence policy in the UK, and one reason it is difficult to assess how much influence they have.
markScheme: Information/expertise and consultations
Access: meetings, committee evidence, advisory bodies
Public campaigns and media / mobilisation
Funding or hospitality (regulated)
Measuring influence: access ≠ influence; counterfactual; anticipated reactions; blocking
questions.modelAnswer: First, lobbyists provide information and expertise, for example in responses to government consultations and evidence to parliamentary committees. Second, they seek access to ministers, civil servants and MPs through meetings and membership of advisory bodies; insider groups have routine access. Third, they run public campaigns, media work and member mobilisation to raise the political cost of ignoring them; outsider groups tend to rely on this. Donations are also used but are regulated by the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000. Assessing influence is difficult because access does not equal influence, because we cannot observe what policy would have been without lobbying, and because influence can work through anticipated reactions or by blocking proposals that never reach the agenda.

questions.q: In Lipsky's analysis (1980), who are 'street-level bureaucrats'?
options: Frontline public workers, such as teachers, police and benefit officers, who deal directly with citizens and exercise discretion
Senior civil servants who advise ministers on policy
Elected local councillors who set local budgets
Independent regulators who set the rules for an industry
questions.why: Lipsky's term refers to frontline workers whose discretion and coping routines shape the policy that citizens experience. Senior advisers are policy-level officials, not the frontline implementers he studied. Elected councillors are politicians, not bureaucrats. Regulators operate at the level of rule setting and oversight and are not the direct service deliverers who are the subject of the analysis.

questions.q: A programme needs 70 independent clearances, and each has a 99% chance of being granted. What is the approximate probability that all are granted?
options: About 1.4%, found by dividing 99% by the 70 steps
About 99%, because a chain is only as weak as its weakest single link
About 30%, found by subtracting 70 × 1% from 100%
questions.why: Independent probabilities multiply, so 0.99 multiplied by itself 70 times is about 0.495. Taking the weakest link treats failure as a single event and ignores that each step adds its own chance of failure. Subtracting 70 × 1% adds the failure probabilities as if the failures never overlapped, which gives 30% and understates the true joint probability of success. Dividing by the number of steps gives about 1.4%, an arithmetic step with no basis in probability theory.

questions.q: Compare top-down and bottom-up approaches to policy implementation, with one example author for each.
markScheme: Top-down: central goals, hierarchy; example Pressman and Wildavsky / Mazmanian and Sabatier / Hogwood and Gunn
Failure explained by complexity, unclear goals, insufficient resources
Bottom-up: street-level discretion (Lipsky)
Implementation as policy making by frontline
Evaluation: strengths/limits of each or Matland's synthesis
questions.modelAnswer: Top-down approaches treat policy as set by decision makers at the centre and judge implementation by how far outcomes match those goals. Pressman and Wildavsky (1973) argued that failures arise from the complexity of joint action, since many agreements must all be reached, and Hogwood and Gunn listed conditions for perfect implementation such as clear objectives and adequate resources. Bottom-up approaches start from frontline workers. Lipsky (1980) showed that street-level bureaucrats exercise discretion under heavy caseloads and limited resources, developing routines and rationing, so the policy as delivered is in effect made at the frontline. Top-down analysis highlights democratic accountability and design; bottom-up highlights the reality of delivery. Matland (1995) suggested that which is more useful depends on conflict and ambiguity.

questions.q: Compare Lindblom's incrementalism, Kingdon's multiple streams approach and Baumgartner and Jones's punctuated equilibrium as explanations of policy change. Illustrate with an example from British or other public policy.
markScheme: Explains each theory accurately with author/date
Lindblom: successive limited comparisons, small steps; explains stability, weak on sudden change
Kingdon: streams, windows, entrepreneurs; explains timing and agenda access
Baumgartner and Jones: stability plus punctuation, policy monopolies, attention, venue
Compares scope: what each explains and what it leaves out
Applies to an example (e.g. smoke-free legislation, Scotland 2006 then England 2007)
Evaluation: testability, relationships between theories, reasoned judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
These theories address different parts of the same puzzle: why policy usually changes slowly but sometimes changes dramatically.

Lindblom (1959) argued that policy makers cannot analyse every alternative, so they proceed by successive limited comparisons and small adjustments to the status quo. This explains the stability and the continuity of most budgets and programmes and the importance of bargaining among actors, but it struggles to account for large changes, and it offers little help in explaining why some issues reach the agenda at all.

Kingdon (1984), building on the garbage can model, treated problems, policies and politics as three separate streams. A policy window opens when a problem becomes pressing or the political environment changes, for example after a focusing event or election, and policy entrepreneurs who have developed solutions couple the streams. The approach explains the timing of agenda access and why solutions often come before problems, but it is less precise about when windows open or what counts as success.

Baumgartner and Jones (1993) argued that policy is marked by long periods of equilibrium maintained by policy monopolies, in which a dominant group controls the policy image and the venue, interrupted by bursts of rapid change when attention shifts and new venues or images are mobilised. This accommodates both incrementalism (most of the time) and large shifts (occasionally), and predicts a distribution with many small changes and a few large ones.

An example is smoke-free legislation. For many years smoking policy changed slowly, with voluntary agreements. As evidence on second-hand smoke accumulated, the policy image shifted from a matter of personal choice to a public health and workplace issue. Scotland legislated in 2006, which provided a policy model and made the idea politically feasible elsewhere; England followed in 2007, and Wales and Northern Ireland also introduced their own restrictions. In punctuated equilibrium terms, the change in image and venue broke the existing monopoly. In Kingdon's terms, the problem stream (evidence), the policy stream (a worked-out ban) and the politics stream (public support and a favourable political climate) came together. Lindblom would stress the earlier incremental steps, such as voluntary codes and restrictions in specific places, but could not by itself explain the step to a comprehensive ban.

Overall, the theories are complementary. Lindblom describes the normal mode, Baumgartner and Jones explain why the normal mode sometimes breaks down, and Kingdon provides the micro-level story of how an opportunity is seized. None is easily falsified, and their strengths differ: Baumgartner and Jones can be tested with data on the distribution of budget changes, while Kingdon's framework is better as a lens for case studies.

questions.q: Who has most influence over public policy: the public, politicians, lobbyists or bureaucrats? Discuss with reference to theory and evidence.
markScheme: Frames the question and defines influence
Public opinion: evidence for and against responsiveness (Page and Shapiro; Gilens and Page; thermostatic)
Politicians: formal authority, constraints (veto players, blame avoidance, mandates)
Lobbyists: insider/outsider, Olson, Baumgartner et al.; difficulty of measuring influence
Bureaucrats: expertise, implementation (Lipsky, Pressman and Wildavsky), principal–agent
Interactions and context (issue salience, institutions)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Influence over policy is shared and varies by issue, stage and institutional context, so a single answer is unlikely to be right. It helps to separate agenda setting, decision and implementation.

The public has formal influence through elections and referendums, and there is evidence of responsiveness. Page and Shapiro (1983) found that US policy changes were more often congruent than not with earlier shifts in opinion, and Wlezien's thermostatic model shows opinion and policy interacting. However, voters are often poorly informed and issues have low salience (Downs, 1957; Converse, 1964), opinion can be shaped by elites (Zaller, 1992), and Gilens and Page (2014) argued that average citizens had little independent influence on US policy once elites and organised groups were taken into account, although this is contested. The ending of the death penalty for murder in Great Britain (suspended in 1965, abolished permanently in 1969) shows policy running ahead of opinion.

Politicians hold formal authority and decide. Their influence is shaped by their goals (re-election, office, policy) and by constraints: veto players (Tsebelis, 2002), coalition bargaining, party discipline, courts and the desire to avoid blame (Weaver, 1986). In the UK a majority government has considerable power, as at the 2024 general election when about 63% of seats followed from 33.7% of votes, but ministers depend on others for information and delivery.

Lobbyists can influence through information, access and campaigns, and insider groups routinely shape detail. Olson (1965) predicts that concentrated interests are better organised than diffuse ones. But the evidence on influence is mixed: Baumgartner et al. (2009) found that resources did not clearly predict success and that defending the status quo mattered more, and measuring influence is difficult because access is not the same as influence. Lobbyists may be most effective at blocking change or shaping implementation details.

Bureaucrats supply expertise and manage implementation. In principal–agent terms they have an information advantage over ministers, and Lipsky (1980) argued that street-level discretion means frontline workers effectively make policy as delivered. Pressman and Wildavsky (1973) showed how complex implementation can undermine intended policy. Against this, officials are constrained by law, ministerial direction and the civil service code.

Conclusion: no single actor dominates. Politicians have the final formal say, but they are constrained, depend on others and respond to opinion and organised interests in different ways depending on salience. Where an issue is highly salient, public opinion and politicians are more important; on low-salience technical issues, organised interests and officials have more room. The best answer treats influence as a relationship among actors that varies by stage: agenda setting (opinion, entrepreneurs, interests), decision (politicians, veto players) and implementation (bureaucrats).
